note: The paraglottic space's definition carves its lateral boundary as the thyrohyoid membrane (parameter 1), and the pre-epiglottic space's accepted definition carves the thyrohyoid membrane as its anterior boundary. Operational test (Law 8): remove the thyrohyoid membrane now and the mapped compartment loses its lateral boundary - the staging landmark no longer operates as the bounded fat plane. Not identity (space vs band) and not purpose (Law 8c). Same boundary line as the laryngeal-inlet edges advanced in this family.
The trachea depends on vagal innervation for mucociliary clearance control and smooth muscle tone regulation; removing the vagus nerve stops these functions.
The surgical landmark depends on the conceptual map for identification.

The thyroepiglottic ligament connects the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage. Remove the thyroid cartilage and the ligament loses its inferior anchor — it ceases to operate. [3 test] DEPENDS_ON: removing thyroid cartilage now stops the ligament from operating. [2 direction] Ligament points to thyroid cartilage as a required component.

The laryngeal inlet is the opening connecting the oropharynx to the laryngeal vestibule, bounded by the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, and arytenoid cartilages. These are all parts of the larynx, and the inlet is the spatial region between them within the laryngeal boundary.

The supraglottis definition explicitly carves the false vocal folds (ventricular folds above the true vocal folds) as parameter 1 of the structures it includes. Vestibular-fold maps that same structure. The fold is a part contained within the supraglottic region. CONTAINS test passes: Y is a part inside X. Direction: whole (supraglottis) to part (vestibular-fold).

The thyroarytenoid muscle's accepted definition explicitly states its subdivisions: 'thyroidarytenoid (muscular) portion and vocalis (medial) portion.' The vocalis muscle IS the medial subdivision of the thyroarytenoid muscle — it is not a separate muscle but a portion of one. The vocalis is literally contained within the thyroarytenoid. CONTAINS direction: thyroarytenoid-muscle (whole) to vocalis-muscle (part).
The trachea depends on the cricotracheal membrane for its superior attachment to the cricoid cartilage; removing it disconnects the trachea from the laryngeal skeleton.

The laryngeal saccule is a blind mucosal pouch extending upward within the larynx, between the vocalis muscle and thyroid cartilage lamina, reaching toward the hyoid bone. It is anatomically contained within the laryngeal framework. CONTAINS test: the saccule occupies a defined position inside the larynx's structural territory, bounded laterally by the thyroid cartilage and medially by the vocalis muscle.

The thyroepiglottic ligament's defined function is to connect the epiglottic apex to the thyroid cartilage. Remove the epiglottis and the ligament has no anchor — it ceases to operate. [3 test] DEPENDS_ON: removing epiglottis now stops thyroepiglottic ligament from operating because it requires the epiglottis as an attachment point. [2 direction] The dependent ligament points to what it needs (epiglottis).

The hypopharynx accepted definition states it 'maps the inferior-most portion of the pharynx, extending from the inferior border of the hyoid bone to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage where it continues as the esophagus.' The larynx definition lists its functional compartments as 'supraglottis, glottis, and subglottis' (parameter 5). The hypopharynx is the anatomical space immediately surrounding and inferior to the larynx — it is not contained within the larynx. Actually, this should be DERIVED_FROM or a different type. Let me reconsider.

The supraglottis definition maps 'the region of the larynx above the vocal folds' and its structures include 'the epiglottis.' The vallecula sits on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, which is itself within the supraglottic region. The vallecula is therefore a landmark within the supraglottic anatomical territory — it lies superior to the vocal folds and is part of the epiglottic component of the supraglottis.

The aryepiglottic-fold definition explicitly carves the corniculate cartilage at the apex of each fold as parameter 2 (the contained cartilage). The corniculate-cartilage IS that cartilage — a literal anatomical part of the fold. CONTAINS test passes: Y is a part inside X. Direction: whole (aryepiglottic-fold) to part (corniculate-cartilage).

The vagus-nerve accepted definition explicitly lists 'the superior laryngeal branch — divides at the inferior vagal ganglion into internal laryngeal (sensory) and external laryngeal (motor) divisions' as parameter 2. The superior-laryngeal-nerve is an anatomical component (branch) of the vagus nerve, mapped within the vagus construct's own parameter structure. This is a structural containment: the vagus nerve's definition carves the SLN as one of its explicit parameters.

The pharynx accepted definition explicitly lists 'the superior-to-inferior divisions — nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx/hypopharynx...' as parameter (1). The hypopharynx is the inferior division of the pharynx construct. Per edge lessons for CONCEPT anatomical entries, explicit parameters support CONTAINS. Type: CONTAINS ✓, Direction: whole (pharynx) to part (hypopharynx) ✓, Test: pharynx definition names hypopharynx as its inferior division ✓, Object level: both are anatomical CONCEPT entries ✓, Sense: pinned to pharynx definition's parameter (1) ✓

The vocal folds definition explicitly states they consist of the vocalis muscle covered by epithelium and lined by lamina propria. The vocalis muscle is a literal physical tissue component of the vocal fold — it is not a separate organ but a tissue layer within the folded structure.

The saccule's definition carves its origin as the anterior recess of the laryngeal ventricle. Removal test: remove the laryngeal ventricle and the saccule ceases to exist — it is the anterior pouch of that ventricle, not an independent structure. The saccule is constitutively dependent on the ventricle as its point of origin.

The cricothyroid joint is the synovial articulation between the cricoid cartilage and the thyroid cartilage. Operational DEPENDS_ON test (Law 8): remove the thyroid cartilage and the joint loses one of its two articulating surfaces — it cannot function to tilt the thyroid cartilage forward or tense the vocal folds. The joint's defined role requires both cartilages to exist. Not identity (the joint is an articulation between two distinct cartilages).
Per the laryngeal vestibule definition, the laryngeal ventricle (the recess between vestibular and vocal folds) lies within the vestibule's boundaries.

The vocal process is defined as a triangular projection on the superior aspect of the arytenoid cartilages lamina where the vocalis muscle inserts. The arytenoid definition (parameter 2) explicitly lists the vocal process as an anterior projection serving as the posterior attachment of the vocal fold. A cartilaginous projection is a literal physical part of the cartilage.

The laryngeal vestibule is a supraglottic region within the larynx, bounded above by the laryngeal inlet and below by the vocal folds. It is a spatial compartment contained within the laryngeal framework.
The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle serves the vocal folds as their sole abductor — pulling the muscular process to rotate the arytenoid and open the glottis during inspiration.
The surgical landmark construct contains the specific attachment as a mapped instance.

The vocal fold definition (from accepted anatomy) lists the thyroarytenoid muscle as a layer within the vocal fold structure. The thyroarytenoid forms the muscular bulk of the vocal fold, with its vocalis subdivision as the medial portion. The muscle is a literal anatomical part of the vocal fold. CONTAINS direction: vocal-fold (whole) to thyroarytenoid-muscle (part).

The vallecula maps shallow depressions on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, bounded anteriorly by the epiglottis itself. The accepted vallecula definition carves it as 'the paired shallow depressions between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis,' with the epiglottic surface forming its anterior boundary. A depression on the surface of a structure is a part of that structure — the vallecula is a mucosal depression carved into the epiglottis. [3 test] CONTAINS test: is vallecula literally a part of epiglottis? Yes — it is a defined mucosal depression on the epiglottic surface, not adjacent to it but a feature of it. Direction: epiglottis (whole) CONTAINS vallecula (part).
The conceptual map contains the surgical construct as a mapped instance.

The hypopharynx definition maps the inferior division of the pharynx including the 'laryngeal inlet (the opening from the oropharynx into the laryngopharynx bounded by the epiglottis and arytenoids).' The vallecula is the depression on the epiglottis that forms the anterior boundary of the laryngeal inlet — it is a structural component of the hypopharynx's defined boundary. The vallecula is anatomically within the hypopharyngeal region and is one of the hypopharynx's four subsites' boundary landmarks.

The pharynx accepted definition explicitly lists 'the superior-to-inferior divisions — nasopharynx, oropharynx (behind the oral cavity, between the soft palate and epiglottis), and laryngopharynx/hypopharynx...' as parameter (1). Per edge lessons for CONCEPT anatomical entries, explicit parameters support CONTAINS. The oropharynx is the middle division of the pharynx construct. Type: CONTAINS ✓, Direction: whole (pharynx) to part (oropharynx) ✓, Test: pharynx definition names oropharynx as its middle division ✓, Object level: both are anatomical CONCEPT entries ✓, Sense: pinned to pharynx definition's parameter (1) ✓
The cricothyroid muscle serves the vocal folds by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward, elongating and tensing the vocal folds for phonation. It is the primary tensor of the vocal folds.

The thyrohyoid membrane's accepted scope is to map the band that suspends the larynx from the hyoid, and its carving pins its superior attachment as the hyoid body and greater horns. Operational test (Law 8): remove the hyoid bone now and the membrane loses its superior anchor — a band that exists to suspend the larynx from a bone that is gone no longer suspends it, so the construct ceases to operate as its carving names it. This is the same attachment-dependency kind the board accepted for the ligament and muscle edges in this batch (the structure's defined role requires the structure it is anchored to). Direction: the dependent membrane points to the bone it needs. Not identity (the membrane is fibrous tissue, not bone) and not purpose (Law 8c).

The thyrohyoid membrane definition (parameter 3) states it 'opens into a slit-like interval (the thyrohyoid hiatus) through which the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels pass.' The internal laryngeal nerve is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. This nerve is structurally within the thyrohyoid membrane's mapped territory, piercing through it.
The rima glottidis is the slit-like opening between the vocal folds, the dynamic aperture within the laryngeal cavity whose dimensions determine airflow resistance during phonation and respiration.

The larynx definition (accepted v1, parameter 1) explicitly carves the cricoid cartilage as part of its cartilaginous framework. The cricotracheal membrane connects the inferior border of the cricoid lamina to the first tracheal ring — it is a structural boundary of the larynx framework, not an external structure. The membrane is part of the laryngeal construct because it is attached to and defined by the cricoid, which is a defined laryngeal component. Direction: whole (larynx) to part (cricotracheal membrane). The edge relates the two concepts as they are carved, not what they map.

The thyroarytenoid muscle's accepted definition carves its innervation as 'recurrent laryngeal nerve supplying both portions.' Removal test: remove the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the thyroarytenoid muscle loses all innervation — it cannot contract, so it ceases to operate as the muscle that modulates vocal fold tension. The nerve is a required component for the muscle's function. This is constitutive dependency, not identity (muscle is tissue, nerve is signaling) or purpose (Law 8c). Direction correct: dependent (muscle) points to what it needs (nerve). [3 test; 2 direction; 4 object level]

The laryngeal vestibule definition lists the vestibular folds as its inferior boundary ('below the free edges of the true vocal folds' and the vestibular folds separate the laryngeal inlet from the vocal folds). The vestibular folds are within the vestibule's boundaries — the vestibule extends from the laryngeal inlet down to the vocal folds, with the vestibular folds positioned within this chamber between the inlet and the laryngeal ventricle.
Per the laryngeal vestibule definition, the pre-epiglottic space (anterior to the epiglottis) lies within the vestibule's boundaries.

The superior laryngeal nerve is a CONCEPT mapping a branch of the vagus that supplies the larynx. Its definition states the internal branch 'pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to become the internal laryngeal nerve, providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds,' and the external branch 'descends on the inferior pharyngeal constrictor to supply the cricothyroid muscle.' These branches physically traverse the laryngeal framework — the nerve is a literal anatomical structure within the larynx's anatomical territory. CONTAINS direction: larynx (whole) to superior-laryngeal-nerve (part).

The conus elasticus definition (parameter 4) states it is 'continuous superiorly with the cricothyroid membrane and with the vocal ligaments (which form its free upper borders).' The vocal ligament is literally the free superior margin of the conus elasticus, making it a structural part of the conus elasticus construct.

The supraglottis definition explicitly includes the laryngeal ventricles as one of its structures. The saccule extends from the anterior portion of the ventricle and occupies the supraglottic space between the vestibular and vocal folds. CONTAINS test: the saccule is a part within the supraglottic territory.
The larynx depends on the recurrent laryngeal nerve for motor innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid; removal causes bilateral vocal fold paralysis.

The cricothyroid-joint definition carves the lateral cricothyroid ligament as parameter 3 of its ligamentous support, and the joint capsule as parameter 2. The cricothyroid-membrane is the fibrous sheet whose boundaries include the cricothyroid joint capsules laterally (per the cricothyroid-membrane definition). But this is not a CONTAINS — the membrane is external to the joint. Striking this.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve serves the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle by providing its motor innervation, enabling the muscle to abduct the vocal folds.

The accepted quadrangular membrane definition lists the hyoepiglottic ligament as its thickened superior edge — a thickening of the membrane's own fibrous substance, not a separate structure bounding it. The ligament's own accepted carving confirms the relationship: it 'forms the anterior boundary of the quadrangular membrane', i.e. it is tissue of the membrane itself. CONTAINS test (Law 10): is the ligament literally a part inside the membrane? Yes — the same way the board accepted the corniculate cartilage as a part inside the aryepiglottic fold (apex cartilage within the fold's substance) and the vocal ligament as a part inside the vocal fold. This is not the boundary case struck for epiglottis/vallecula: there a separate structure (its own cartilage, its own map) bounded the region; here the 'boundary' is the parent's own thickened tissue, so the part is inside the map. Direction: whole (membrane) to part (ligament).

The cricothyroid muscle's accepted definition carves its innervation as 'external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.' Removal test: remove the superior laryngeal nerve and the cricothyroid muscle loses all innervation — it cannot contract, ceasing to operate as the primary tensor of the vocal folds. Constitutive dependency. Direction correct.

The thyroarytenoid muscle's accepted definition carves its origin as 'anterior inner surface of the thyroid cartilage angle.' Removal test: remove the thyroid cartilage and the muscle loses its anterior anchor — it cannot operate as the muscle spanning thyroid to arytenoid. Constitutive attachment dependency. Direction correct.

The laryngocele's definition carves its origin as distension of the laryngeal saccule (parameter 1), and the laryngeal ventricle's accepted definition carves the saccule as the blind pouch of the ventricle's anterior portion (parameters 2 and 3). Operational test (Law 8): remove the laryngeal ventricle now and the saccule with it - the mapped cystic distension has nothing to distend and the construct ceases to operate. Not identity (a distension of a pouch is not the pouch or the ventricle) and not purpose (Law 8c): the laryngocele is a clinical entity that needs the ventricle's saccule to exist.

The vagus-nerve definition explicitly carves recurrent laryngeal branches as parameter 3: right hooks under subclavian, left under aortic arch, both ascending in tracheoesophageal groove. The recurrent-laryngeal-nerve IS those branches — a genuine anatomical branch of the vagus nerve, constituting a literal part of the parent nerve. CONTAINS test passes: Y is a part inside X. Direction: whole (vagus-nerve) to part (recurrent-laryngeal-nerve).

The cricothyroid membrane definition (parameter 2) explicitly lists 'the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal vessels passing on its deep surface' as a component relationship. This nerve runs on the deep surface of the membrane and is a structural element within the cricothyroid membrane's carved territory.

Per the vocal ligament definition: 'the free superior margin of the cricothyroid membrane.' Per the cricothyroid membrane definition: 'its free superior border thickens into the vocal ligament.' The ligament is literally the thickened superior edge of the membrane.

The cricothyroid-membrane definition carves the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve passing on its deep surface. The cricothyroid-muscle definition says it inserts on the inferior horn and lower border of the thyroid cartilage, and originates from the cricoid arch. The cricothyroid-muscle's origin is the cricoid cartilage (separate entry), and it inserts on the thyroid cartilage — it does NOT sit inside the membrane. The nerve passes ON the membrane's surface. This is not a genuine CONTAINS. I should file a proper edge or skip.

The cricothyroid joint is the articulation between the inferior horns of the thyroid cartilage and facets on the cricoid cartilage. Remove the cricoid cartilage and the joint loses one of its two articular surfaces — it ceases to operate. [3 test] DEPENDS_ON: removing cricoid stops the joint from operating. [2 direction] Joint points to cricoid as required component.

The thyroepiglottic ligament connects the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage and is listed in the larynx definition's parameter (1) as part of the cartilaginous framework: 'thyroid, cricoid, and epiglottic cartilages plus the paired arytenoid cartilages.' The ligament is the connective tissue component between two of these framework cartilages, making it a constituent part of the laryngeal structure.

The cricothyroid muscle inserts on the inferior horn and lower border of the thyroid cartilage. Remove the thyroid cartilage and the muscle loses its insertion — it ceases to operate. [3 test] DEPENDS_ON: removing thyroid cartilage stops the cricothyroid muscle from operating. [2 direction] Muscle points to thyroid cartilage as a required component.

The carina is the midline cartilaginous ridge at the inferior terminus of the tracheal lumen where it bifurcates (definition parameter 2). The carina is literally a physical part of the tracheal structure, not a separate organ.

The cricothyroid membrane's superior border is the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage. Operational DEPENDS_ON test (Law 8): remove the thyroid cartilage and the membrane loses its superior anchor — it can no longer function as the fibrous sheet between the two cartilages. The membrane's defined role requires both attachment points. Not identity and not purpose (Law 8c).

The supraglottis definition explicitly carves the laryngeal ventricles (spaces between false and true vocal folds) as parameter 1 of the structures it includes. Laryngeal-ventricle maps that space. The ventricle is a part contained within the supraglottic region. CONTAINS test passes: Y is a part inside X. Direction: whole (supraglottis) to part (laryngeal-ventricle).

The larynx definition carves its neural supply as 'superior laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches of the vagus.' Removal test: remove the vagus nerve and all laryngeal innervation is lost — the larynx cannot produce voiced sound or manage the airway, ceasing to operate as the construct maps it. The vagus is the substrate for all laryngeal neural control. This is constitutive dependency. Direction correct: dependent (larynx) points to what it needs (vagus nerve). [3 test; 2 direction; 4 object level]

Law 10 test: the laryngeal framework is literally a part inside the larynx — a material composite (the six cartilages with their inter-cartilaginous ligaments and membranes) physically within the organ, not a boundary of a region. The larynx's own accepted definition lists it as parameter (1) 'the cartilaginous framework — thyroid, cricoid, and epiglottic cartilages plus the paired arytenoid cartilages'; a parent definition that lists a component supports CONTAINS, the same line as the six accepted component CONTAINS edges. Distinct from the struck supraglottis CONTAINS epiglottis: there the epiglottis is the boundary of the supraglottis region, not a part within it; here the framework is a structural member of the organ. Sense pinned to the accepted larynx and laryngeal-framework definitions. Whole to part, direction correct (Law 18b-ii 2).

The cricotracheal membrane is a fibrous band bridging cricoid to first tracheal ring; it lies below the larynx and is not a component of the laryngeal framework. CONTAINS requires literal part inside X; this is anatomically outside the larynx. The edge direction is wrong; the membrane belongs to the tracheal region, not contained by larynx.

The larynx definition lists the paired arytenoid cartilages as part of the cartilaginous framework (parameter 1). The arytenoid cartilages are literally physical parts contained within the laryngeal structure.

The corniculate cartilages sit atop the apices of the arytenoid cartilages. Operational DEPENDS_ON test (Law 8): remove the arytenoid cartilages and the corniculate cartilages lose their foundation — they have no independent structural position without the arytenoid apices they rest upon. The corniculate's defined role (forming part of the posterior laryngeal inlet) requires the arytenoid position as its base. Not identity (elastic cartilage on top of cartilage — two distinct structures with different positions and definitions).
The larynx contains the vocal folds as integral structures within the glottic compartment — the paired mucosal folds that vibrate to produce voiced sound.

The interarytenoid muscle's accepted definition carves its innervation as 'recurrent laryngeal nerve.' Removal test: remove the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the muscle loses all innervation — it cannot contract, ceasing to operate as an adductor of the arytenoids. Constitutive dependency. Direction correct.
The larynx contains the recurrent laryngeal nerve as its primary motor innervation: the branch supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid.
The trachea depends on the recurrent laryngeal nerve for parasympathetic innervation and motor control of trachealis muscle; removal stops these functions.

The corniculate cartilage (cartilago corniculata) is a component of the laryngeal cartilaginous framework as defined by the larynx entry's parameter (1): 'thyroid, cricoid, and epiglottic cartilages plus the paired arytenoid cartilages.' The corniculate cartilages sit atop the arytenoid apices within the aryepiglottic folds, forming part of the posterior laryngeal inlet. The definition's parameter (1) establishes the larynx's cartilaginous framework, and the corniculate cartilage is one of the structures within that framework.

The laryngeal inlet definition explicitly lists the aryepiglottic folds as one of its boundaries: 'laterally by the aryepiglottic folds' is a boundary parameter. The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral walls of the laryngeal inlet and are a constituent structural element of it. The inlet definition also lists 'the aryepiglottic folds contract inward during swallowing to close the inlet' — they are integral to the inlet construct.

The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle's accepted definition carves its innervation as 'recurrent laryngeal nerve.' Removal test: remove the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the muscle loses all innervation — it cannot contract, ceasing to operate as an adductor of the vocal folds. Constitutive dependency. Direction correct.

The laryngeal inlet's anterior boundary is the epiglottis. Operational DEPENDS_ON test (Law 8): remove the epiglottis and the inlet loses its anterior boundary — the protective mechanism (epiglottis tilting posteriorly during swallowing to close the inlet) cannot operate. The inlet's defined role requires the epiglottis as its anterior landmark. Not identity (the inlet is a mapped opening, the epiglottis is a cartilage).

The vocal-fold definition maps the layered microstructure whose core is the vocal ligament. The vocal-ligament definition explicitly states it is 'the free superior margin of the cricothyroid membrane, forming the elastic fiber core of the vocal fold.' The ligament is literally a structural part inside the vocal fold construct — the stiff elastic scaffold upon which the mucosal wave oscillates. The vocal fold contains the ligament as its core structural element, making this a genuine part-whole CONTAINS relation.

The vallecula maps the shallow depression between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, which is structurally part of the laryngeal inlet region. The larynx definition (parameters 1-5) maps the organ system housing the vocal folds and their musculature, and the vallecula is a landmark within this system used in airway management — the epiglottis, laryngeal inlet, and vallecula are all listed as anatomical landmarks in airway management within the larynx definition itself.

The aryepiglottic-fold definition explicitly carves the cuneiform cartilage embedded within the fold's substance as parameter 2 (the contained cartilage). The cuneiform-cartilage IS that cartilage — a literal anatomical part of the fold. CONTAINS test passes: Y is a part inside X. Direction: whole (aryepiglottic-fold) to part (cuneiform-cartilage).

The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the superior border and apex of the epiglottis to the hyoid bone, forming the anterior boundary of the quadrangular membrane. The epiglottis definition lists 'a superior connection to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament' as one of its five parameters. This is a part-to-whole relation: the ligament is a constituent attachment of the epiglottis construct.

The laryngeal inlet's posterior boundary is the arytenoid cartilages. Operational DEPENDS_ON test (Law 8): remove the arytenoid cartilages and the inlet loses its posterior boundary — the boundaries that define the inlet (anterior: epiglottis, lateral: aryepiglottic folds, posterior: arytenoids) cannot be maintained. The inlet's defined role requires the arytenoid position. Not identity (the inlet is a mapped opening between structures, not the structures themselves).
The carina is the structural point from which the bronchi emerge — the carina's anatomical domain includes the bronchial bifurcation, making the bronchi its subordinate structures.

The vocal fold definition lists the vocalis muscle (intrinsic laryngeal muscle) as part of the layered microstructure — parameter 1 of the definition. The vocalis muscle is literally a physical component of the vocal fold tissue, not a separate organ.

The stylohyoid ligament's definition carves its inferior attachment as the greater horn of the hyoid bone (parameter 1) and its function as suspending the hyoid from the styloid process (parameter 3). Operational test (Law 8): remove the hyoid bone now and the ligament loses its inferior anchor - a band connecting the skull base to a bone that is gone no longer suspends it and ceases to operate. Not identity (fibrous band vs bone) and not purpose (Law 8c). Same attachment line as the standing thyrohyoid-membrane DEPENDS_ON hyoid-bone in this family.
The surgical construct depends on the conceptual map for identification during airway procedures.
The conceptual map is a specific instance of the surgical construct's landmark mapping.

The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the epiglottis to the hyoid bone and is referenced in the larynx definition's parameter (1) establishing the cartilaginous framework. Though the hyoid is not a laryngeal cartilage, the hyoepiglottic ligament is a laryngeal structure insofar as it attaches the epiglottis (a laryngeal cartilage) to the hyoid, forming the anterior suspension of the larynx. It is a standard laryngeal anatomical landmark in airway management and laryngeal surgery.
The carina is the cartilaginous ridge at the inferior terminus of the laryngeal boundary where the trachea bifurcates, a key landmark within the laryngeal construct's spatial domain.

The laryngeal-inlet definition carves the arytenoid cartilages as parameter 1 (boundaries posteriorly by the arytenoid cartilages). The arytenoid cartilages are an explicit anatomical component named in the inlet's carving.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a CONCEPT mapping a nerve branch that enters and runs within the larynx. Its definition states it 'ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove between the trachea and esophagus, entering the larynx posterior to the inferior constrictor' and innervates all intrinsic laryngeal muscles. The nerve physically enters the laryngeal framework — it is a literal anatomical structure within the larynx's anatomical territory. CONTAINS direction: larynx (whole) to recurrent-laryngeal-nerve (part).
The cuneiform cartilage is embedded within the aryepiglottic fold, a component of the laryngeal framework that contributes to laryngeal inlet closure during swallowing.
The carina as the point of tracheal bifurcation depends on the existence of the main bronchi to have meaning; without bronchi there is no bifurcation point.

The laryngeal-inlet definition carves the epiglottis as parameter 1 (boundary anteriorly bounded by the epiglottis). The epiglottis is an explicit anatomical component named in the inlet's own carving.

The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the hyoid bone to the epiglottic apex. Remove the epiglottis and the ligament loses its inferior anchor — it ceases to operate. [3 test] DEPENDS_ON: removing epiglottis now stops hyoepiglottic ligament from operating. [2 direction] Ligament points to epiglottis as a required component.

The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle's accepted definition carves its innervation as 'recurrent laryngeal nerve.' Removal test: remove the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the muscle loses all innervation — it cannot contract, so it ceases to operate as the sole abductor of the vocal folds. Constitutive dependency. Direction correct.

The trachea bifurcates into the main bronchi at the carina (parameter 3 of the trachea definition). The bronchi are literal anatomical parts continuing from the tracheal airway. The trachea definition explicitly maps this connection.

The larynx depends on the superior laryngeal nerve: external branch to cricothyroid muscle and internal branch providing sensory to supraglottis; removal impairs pitch control and supraglottic sensation.

The hypopharynx definition explicitly carves the laryngeal inlet as one of its four subsites in parameter (1): 'the four subsites — postcricoid region; bilateral pyriform sinuses; the posterior pharyngeal wall; and the laryngeal inlet.' For CONCEPT entries mapping anatomy, CONTAINS passes when the definition lists Y as an explicit parameter — the entry IS a map, and the map includes the laryngeal inlet as a mapped component. All 5 items pass: type (CONTAINS), direction (whole to part), test (parameter list shows laryngeal inlet as a subsite of hypopharynx), object level (both CONCEPT maps), sense (laryngeal-inlet used as its accepted definition carves it).

The cricotracheal membrane connects the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage to the first tracheal ring. The larynx definition includes the cricoid cartilage (parameter 1) and the definition of cricotracheal membrane states it connects the cricoid to the first tracheal ring. The cricoid's inferior border is part of the larynx's structural boundary, and the membrane is the fibrous continuation of that boundary. The larynx as a construct maps the organ system whose boundaries extend to include this connecting structure.

The vallecula definition maps it as a shallow depression bounded anteriorly by 'the posterior surface of the epiglottis.' The epiglottis definition maps the leaf-shaped structure whose 'broad lingual surface faces the root of the tongue.' The vallecula is the depression on the lingual (anterior) surface of the epiglottis — it is literally a feature of the epiglottic structure. The epiglottis contains the vallecula as its own surface anatomy, much as a bone contains a groove.

The laryngeal-vestibule definition carves the laryngeal inlet as the superior boundary of the vestibule (above by the laryngeal inlet, epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoid cartilages). The laryngeal-inlet is the opening that forms the superior boundary of the vestibular chamber. The inlet is literally a part of the vestibular construct's boundary structure. CONTAINS test passes: Y is a part of X. Direction: whole (laryngeal-vestibule) to part (laryngeal-inlet).

The cricothyroid membrane's inferior border is the superior border of the cricoid cartilage. Operational DEPENDS_ON test (Law 8): remove the cricoid cartilage now and the membrane loses its inferior anchor — it can no longer function as the fibrous sheet between the two cartilages that serves as the emergency airway landmark. The membrane's defined role requires both attachment points to exist. Not identity (the membrane is fibrous tissue, the cricoid is cartilage) and not purpose (Law 8c).

The pharynx accepted definition explicitly lists 'the superior-to-inferior divisions — nasopharynx (behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate), oropharynx..., and laryngopharynx/hypopharynx...' as parameter (1). Per edge lessons for CONCEPT anatomical entries, when an entry's accepted definition lists X as one of its explicit parameters, a CONTAINS edge passes. The nasopharynx is the superior division of the pharynx construct. Type: CONTAINS ✓, Direction: whole (pharynx) to part (nasopharynx) ✓, Test: pharynx definition names nasopharynx as its superior division ✓, Object level: both are anatomical CONCEPT entries ✓, Sense: pinned to pharynx definition's parameter (1) ✓

The cricothyroid muscle originates from the anterior and inferior surface of the cricoid cartilage arch. Remove the cricoid and the muscle loses its origin — it ceases to operate. [3 test] DEPENDS_ON: removing cricoid cartilage stops the cricothyroid muscle from operating. [2 direction] The dependent structure (muscle) points to the required component (cricoid).

The pre-epiglottic space lies anterior to the epiglottis, which is a supraglottic structure. The supraglottis definition lists the epiglottis as one of its primary structures, and the pre-epiglottic space is bounded by the thyroepiglottic ligament (posteriorly) and lies within the supraglottic compartment. It is anatomically part of the supraglottic region assessed in supraglottic cancer staging.
The glottis depends on vagal innervation for vocal fold adduction/abduction via RLN to laryngeal muscles; without vagal input the glottis cannot open or close.

The vocal ligament is the free superior margin of the cricothyroid membrane and forms the elastic core of the vocal fold, which is a component of the laryngeal framework. It is a literal anatomical part within the larynx's cartilaginous and membranous framework, as mapped in laryngology texts.

The laryngeal ventricle is the hourglass-shaped recess between the superior (vestibular) folds and inferior (vocal) folds within the laryngeal cavity. The vocal folds and vestibular folds are both within the larynx (larynx definition parameters 2 and 3), so the ventricle is a spatial region contained within the larynx.
The cricothyroid membrane is a fibrous sheet between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, forming the floor of the laryngeal cavity and a key anatomical landmark within the laryngeal framework.

The hypopharynx definition explicitly lists 'bilateral pyriform sinuses' as one of its four subsites (parameter 1). Piriform-fossa maps the same anatomical structure (piriform fossa = pyriform sinus). The fossa is a subsite contained within the hypopharyngeal region, making this a clear CONTAINS relationship. The piriform-fossa entry itself states it 'belongs to the hypopharyngeal (laryngopharyngeal) region.'
The trachea extends from the larynx at C6 to the carina at T4–T5. The laryngeal boundary begins at the larynx, and the trachea is the continuation of the airway through this region.

The trachea construct maps the cartilaginous tube from the larynx to the lungs. The cricotracheal membrane connects the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage to the superior border of the first tracheal ring. This membrane is the fibrous junction at the larynx-trachea boundary. The first tracheal ring is part of the trachea construct, and the membrane attaches to it as its superior boundary. The membrane is the transitional structure at the tracheal entrance, contained within the tracheal construct as its superior boundary structure.

The esophagus's accepted definition carves its wall layers including the myenteric plexus innervated by vagal efferents. Removal test: remove the vagus nerve and the esophagus loses all parasympathetic innervation — peristalsis is disrupted, the lower esophageal sphincter cannot relax, and the organ ceases to operate as a transport conduit. Direction correct.

The thyroepiglottic ligament attaches to the epiglottic apex and lateral borders, forming an integral structural component of the epiglottis construct. The epiglottis definition lists 'a stalk fixed to the thyroid cartilage by the thyroepiglottic ligament' as one of its five parameters. This is a part-to-whole relation: the ligament is a constituent of the epiglottic structure, not merely adjacent to it.
The larynx contains the epiglottis as a leaf-shaped cartilaginous guard at the laryngeal inlet, positioned superior to the glottis.

The vallecula maps depressions on the lingual surface of the epiglottis. The epiglottis is part of the larynx (larynx CONTAINS epiglottis accepted). A feature of a part is contained by the whole. [3 test] CONTAINS test: vallecula is literally a part of the larynx's anatomy — it is a mucosal depression on the epiglottic surface, which is a laryngeal structure. [2 direction] Larynx (whole) CONTAINS vallecula (part).

The supraglottis definition explicitly lists the epiglottis as one of its primary structures: '(1) the structures it includes - the epiglottis (leaflet that folds to cover the glottis during swallowing)' is the very first item. The epiglottis is a constituent part of the supraglottic region, making this a clear CONTAINS relation.

The thyroarytenoid muscle's accepted definition carves its insertion as 'lateral surface and muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage.' Removal test: remove the arytenoid cartilage and the muscle loses its posterior anchor — it cannot operate as the muscle spanning thyroid to arytenoid. Constitutive attachment dependency. Direction correct.

The cricothyroidotomy is the emergency surgical airway created THROUGH the cricothyroid membrane. Operational DEPENDS_ON test (Law 8): remove the cricothyroid membrane and the procedure has no access route — the incision or puncture targets this specific membrane between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. Without this membrane as the anatomical landmark and access point, the cricothyroidotomy procedure cannot operate as defined. Not identity and not purpose (Law 8c).
The conceptual map SERVES the surgical construct as a landmark for procedural execution.
The larynx construct contains the pre-epiglottic space as a part: the fat-filled region anterior to the epiglottis is anatomically situated within the supraglottic compartment of the larynx.

The trachea (cartilaginous tube C6 to T4-T5) terminates at the carina where it bifurcates into the bronchi. Anatomically, the bronchi arise from the inferior termination of the trachea — the carina is the transition point. The bronchi are the direct anatomical continuation of the tracheal lumen. The trachea's structural design (16-20 C-shaped rings, mucociliary escalator) is adapted to deliver air to the branching bronchial tree. The bronchi could not exist without the tracheal conduit above them.
The bronchus depends on vagal innervation for bronchial smooth muscle tone control; removing vagal input stops parasympathetic bronchoconstriction and sympathetic bronchodilation regulation.
